sections.title: A seed. A ticket. A whole world.
sections.rule: A little seed is looking for a place to belong.
lines: Come along, little seed. There is a whole world waiting beyond this station.
But where could you make a home? Let us follow the clues.

sections.title: First, somewhere to stand.
lines: Before a forest, before a river, we need a little ground.
Layers of noise lift the hills. Frequency changes their size; resolution reveals their shape.
A shader gives snow, stone, and shore their own voice.

sections.title: The rain remembers.
lines: Listen. Here comes the rain. Each drop begins a small journey downhill.
Together, the drops carry soil away, then leave it somewhere new.
Near the coast, tides cover the low ground. Even a familiar path can disappear.

sections.title: Not every place feels like home.
lines: Our little seed has found land. But land alone is not enough.
Too steep? Too dry? Warmth and moisture turn a map into a patchwork of possible homes.

sections.title: One seed becomes a story.
lines: Ah, this sheltered patch will do. A branch grows, then branches again.
A tree becomes larger. A forest becomes more crowded. Those are two different stories.
Growth, new seeds, and competition decide which story comes next.

sections.title: There is a world beneath the world.
sections.rule: Density → carve space → mesh in chunks
lines: But wait. What if our world has an inside?
Density tells us where solid ground exists. Subtract a shape, and a cave appears.
Meshing reveals its surface. Chunks let us change one piece without rebuilding the whole world.

sections.title: You cannot see the wind. Until…
lines: A breeze catches another seed. The invisible has left a visible trail.
A vector gives each place a direction and a speed. Particles show us the journey.
A fluid needs another step: pressure correction keeps its flow more consistent.

sections.title: Now, let us look a little closer.
sections.rule: Shape → water → habitat → life · volume & motion
lines: So a world is a conversation: between shape, water, climate, and life.
Our map joins the ideas. The experiments remain separate, so we can see what each rule really does.
Now, let us change one thing at a time.

sections.title: From a story to an experiment
lines: Keep the seed. Keep the camera. Change one rule, and watch.

sections.title: The size of a hill
lines: Watch the frequency slider move. Broad hills become smaller, more closely spaced hills.
The seed stays the same. We are changing the pattern, not rolling a new world.

sections.title: A field is not its mesh
lines: Now keep the field, and change how many points we sample.
More cells reveal detail. They also cost more work.

sections.title: The mountain changes its coat
lines: Only the snow threshold moves. The mountain itself stays still.
A material can explain height without changing geometry.

sections.title: Two rains, one beginning
lines: Both landscapes begin alike. Both receive the same number of simulation steps.
One gets more rain. Ochre shows removed ground; teal shows deposited sediment.
The measurements help us notice changes that a pretty image might hide.

sections.title: Where could the seed settle?
lines: Hold the terrain and temperature still. Let moisture increase.
The habitat labels change. This is a climate classification, not a weather forecast.

sections.title: The inside of a mountain
lines: A sphere, a box, and a noisy volume begin with different density rules.
The slice reveals solid and empty space. Marching cubes follows their boundary.

sections.title: An opening, and a surprise
lines: Watch the cave radius. A small cutter opens a tunnel through the mountain.
Now change the order. Carve first, add a pillar afterward, and solid returns inside the opening.

sections.title: A small edit stays small
lines: One pocket touches nearby chunks. Their meshes rebuild; distant meshes remain.
Local work saves unnecessary work.

sections.title: The price of detail
lines: Increase the voxel resolution. The same rule now produces more triangles.
Compare measured meshing time, not just how smooth the surface looks.

sections.title: Small pieces, more bookkeeping
lines: Smaller chunks can limit an edit, but there are more pieces to manage.
The counters reveal the tradeoff.

sections.title: Many ways to find a surface
lines: Compare the alternatives here. This project implements marching cubes.

sections.title: A direction becomes a journey
lines: Two particle groups travel for the same time, at the same speed.
Turn one field by ninety degrees. Its direction changes; the travel distance does not.

sections.title: Flow needs a little balance
lines: Both grids carry dye. The right grid also corrects its pressure.
Watch the divergence measurement fall. Dye makes motion visible, but it is not water height.

sections.title: A tree, written as a rule
lines: Replace each forward instruction with the same little branching sentence.
Five segments become twenty-five, then one hundred and twenty-five. Grammar depth builds structure; it is not age.

sections.title: Open the branches
lines: Keep the same branches. A wider turn angle opens the crown.

sections.title: Larger does not mean more
lines: Reproduction is off. Growth changes size, while the population stays fixed.

sections.title: A forest has a history
lines: Now allow the right forest to make new seeds.
Both stands can grow, but only one can welcome new seedlings.
Watch births, deaths, and total population. A forest is more than a collection of tree shapes.

sections.title: Room to grow
lines: Crowding can lower health before trees die. Watch the health measurement.

sections.title: The path that comes and goes
lines: The forest holds still while the tide rises. Low ground disappears beneath the water.
The path search must find dry ground, or admit there is no route.
As the tide retreats, a connection can return.

sections.title: A whole world of questions
lines: And here we are again, with a whole world in front of us.
The turning planet brings the ideas together. Its controls do not run one giant physical simulation.
Our seed has taught us how to ask better questions: what changed, what stayed fixed, and why?
Now it is your turn. Which little rule will you change first?
